title: Police raid Starbucks Korea headquarters over 'Tank Day' fiasco
description: South Korean police have raided the national headquarters of Starbucks over defamation claims surrounding a controversial marketing campaign. Starbuck
body: South Korean police have raided the national headquarters of Starbucks over defamation claims surrounding a controversial marketing campaign. Starbucks Korea had in May launched a coffee tumbler promotion called "Tank Day" on the anniversary of the 1980 Gwangju Uprising, where hundreds were believed to have been killed by military forces. Many felt the "tank" was a reference to vehicles deployed to crush pro-democracy protesters and the promotion sparked a mass boycott movement.Starbucks quickly rolled it back, saying it was unintentional but civic groups filed a criminal complaint against the company, demanding the police investigate it for defaming victims of the military dictatorship.Shinsegae Group, which operates Starbucks in Korea, said it had launched an internal investigation into the campaign and concluded that the mistake was unintentional. It added the team that had planned the promotion did not draw the connection to the historical event, and the upper management had failed to spot it as well.In June, Starbucks stores across the country closed for half a day to allow staff to attend history lessons.Shinsegae apologised for the "inappropriate marketing" and said that the Tank Day controversy had led to serious decline in Starbucks sales in South Korea - one of the coffee chain's largest markets.The company also sacked its chief executive. Reports estimate that hundreds were killed by the forces of military dictator Chun Doo-hwan, on what is now remembered as a day of national trauma for South Koreans - and a day held sacred by many in the country. In addition, promotional material for the tumbler used the phrase "tak on the table!", mimicking the sound of an object being slapped on a surface.But "tak" was also the word used in a controversial statement given by police in 1987, describing the death of a student activist in custody.South Korea's president Lee Jae Myung was among those who criticised the campaign, saying it "insults the victims and the bloody struggle" of Gwangju residents.The scandal, which broke during the local elections season, also became a prominent talking point between the two major parties.While the internal ministry under Lee announced a government-level boycott of Starbucks, the opposition leader responded by holding up a Starbucks cup during a speech and accusing the government of overreach.Since then, Starbucks cups have been embraced by right-wing pundits as a symbol of opposition to the Lee Jae-myung government. It has also made appearances in right-wing rallies and livestreams.

schema.headline: Police raid Starbucks Korea headquarters over 'Tank Day' fiasco

title: Russian ballistic missile strike on Kyiv kills at least 17
description: Russia has attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles and drones, killing at least 17 people, as Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said interceptor
body: Russia has attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles and drones, killing at least 17 people, as Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said interceptors "could have saved lives".In one of the deadliest strikes on Kyiv and the capital region this year - which started after midnight on Wednesday - at least 45 people were injured after residential buildings, a railway station and warehouses were hit.Ukraine, who has consistently urged allies for more US-made Patriot missile interceptors to defend against Russian ballistics, has not reported intercepting any of the missiles in the overnight attack.Zelensky added delays in receiving anti-ballistic systems from partners leads to "horrific casualties and destruction".The Russia defence ministry said it had struck logistics hubs and supply centres in Kyiv and the surrounding region."These centres were involved in the storage, delivery of various weapons and military supplies, as well as in the production and distribution of unmanned aerial vehicles," it said.It also said it had hit three cargo vessels "which were transporting weapons and military equipment" near the Black Sea port of Odesa.Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said there were fears people could be trapped under rubble.Ukraine's emergency services said one person had died in the city of Kyiv and at least 16 injured, with a further 16 dead and 29 injured in the wider region.Fires were still being extinguished in five locations across the region on Wednesday, covering an area of approximately 230,000 sq m, it added.The country's air force said in a post on Telegram that Russia had launched 24 ballistic missiles and four anti-ship missiles during the attack on the capital.The air force added that 115 drones had been launched by Russia during the attack and air defence systems intercepted 98 of them.Russia has intensified attacks on Kyiv in recent weeks, while Ukraine has also increased its attacks on Russian civilian infrastructure, including power facilities.Dmitry Milyaev, the governor of Russia's Tula region, said on Wednesday that a drone had crashed into a warehouse of e-commerce giant Wildberries in the region overnight and caused a fire.He said on Telegram that one person had been injured and there had been no deaths reported, with the retailer saying firefighting teams were working at the site and the facility had been evacuated pre-emptively.Ukraine has repeatedly targeted warehouses, including those operated by Wildberries. Five people were killed and 10 wounded in the Moscow region on Tuesday morning in the most recent strikes on warehouses.The day before, Russian officials said seven people were killed and 58 injured after a drone hit a busy beach in the southern Krasnodar region.Ukraine, meanwhile, expressed outrage over a video showing a man chased by a drone in Kherson, calling it a deliberate "hunt" and "safari" targeting civilians.Both sides have denied deliberately targeting civilians.European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Wednesday the EU had received €1.4bn (£1.2bn) from immobilised Russian assets, which would be used to support Ukraine in its war against Russia.

schema.headline: Russian ballistic missile strike on Kyiv kills at least 17

title: Mass funeral in Gaza for 112 Palestinians killed in 2023 Israeli strike
description: Large crowds turned out in Gaza City for a mass funeral for 112 people, mostly women and children, who were killed in an Israeli strike on a residenti
body: Large crowds turned out in Gaza City for a mass funeral for 112 people, mostly women and children, who were killed in an Israeli strike on a residential block in late 2023, early in the Gaza war.The bodies - belonging to members of two extended families - have only recently been recovered from under the rubble in a two-week-long operation.Dramatic footage showed the remains lined up in rows, each victim covered with a Palestinian flag and some with a photo of the dead, before relatives carried them away.The funeral is said to be the biggest of its kind to have taken place in Gaza."I think this is a feeling that was supposed [to be felt], a feeling of pain, grief and loss," said one mourner, Ali Abu Sharia. "After we managed to retrieve them and bury them, perhaps we can be partially relieved despite the pain of loss and all we're still living through."Forty-four children, 38 women and seven people with disabilities were listed among the dead from the Abu Sharia and Hassayna families, who are one clan.They were killed when a residential block in the Sabra neighbourhood of Gaza City was attacked by Israel on 22 November 2023.It was a day of heavy bombardment, six weeks after the 7 October Hamas-led assault on southern Israel, which led to 1,200 people being killed and 251 being taken hostage.The BBC has asked the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) for information on what was targeted but has not yet received a response.Since the start of the war, at least 73,377 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.In Gaza, the recovery work was carried out by the Civil Defence, which operates under the Hamas-run interior ministry. Its efforts have been supported by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC)."We provide material support - literally the gloves, shovels, protective equipment and body bags they use," said Patrick Griffiths, spokesperson for the ICRC."We provide training, supporting them to do their work safely, in line with professional practice ensuring the deceased are treated with dignity. And we've supported them by renting - for hundreds of hours - two of the only excavators available for this work in Gaza.""It's not an answer any family wants to receive - confirmation that your loved one has been killed," Griffiths added. "But it's essential towards them receiving closure and being able to mourn their loss in their own way."Last month, the BBC filmed the start of the operation to uncover bodies in Sabra.  A single bulldozer picked through the rubble and then more delicate work was done by hand."This multi-storey building has been levelled. There were maybe more than 180 civilians inside. Most of them, around 90%, were killed," Civil Defence spokesman Mahmoud Basal said at the time."On that day [of the strikes], the Civil Defence crews couldn't get to the site because it needed co-ordination [with Israel via a third party such as the ICRC] and there was great danger in reaching the area."Relatives of the dead were at the scene to guide the recovery crews during the recovery work. They said they had retrieved as many bodies as they could immediately after the attack and were relieved to be able to give others a proper burial."It's a devastating and sad feeling that resonates with everyone who was here," said Nahed al-Hassayna, as he showed the BBC the rubble of his family's living room."The kids – what did they do?" he asked, holding up the possessions of two of his young relatives. "This was a school backpack for Omar, and this was Ibrahim's shoe. Why? Why were they killed?""I'm the sole survivor of my family," said Yousef Abu Sharia, standing nearby. "Today, I'm talking to you [as] the one who lost my mother, my father, my uncle and my cousins and all my family. I lost them under this rubble."It is believed that dozens more bodies are yet to be recovered at the site.Across the Gaza Strip, thousands more people are unaccounted for.  The remains of many are thought to be under the rubble left by intense Israeli air strikes during the war.

schema.headline: Mass funeral in Gaza for 112 Palestinians killed in 2023 Israeli strike

title: Cameroon's President Biya reshuffles army amid unease at his long stay in Switzerland
description: After an unexpected coup three years ago in neighbouring Gabon, which toppled the Bongo dynasty sending shockwaves across the continent, Cameroon imme
body: After an unexpected coup three years ago in neighbouring Gabon, which toppled the Bongo dynasty sending shockwaves across the continent, Cameroon immediately reshuffled its military leadership.Then, while running for a controversial eighth term in power at last year's presidential election, Biya reshuffled the top brass of the army.Again in June this year, he promoted several members of the defence and security forces to higher ranks.The circumstances under which the latest changes were made have sparked debate, especially among social media users. Biya made the appointments in separate decrees on Monday from the Swiss city of Geneva, where he has been staying since leaving Cameroon on 7 June for what his team described as a "brief private stay".Many in Cameroon have criticised the lack of information about his activities and the uncertainty surrounding the duration of his foreign trip.After last year's election, he promised to name a new cabinet, but has yet to do so. A new post of vice-president that was created this April remains unfilled.During his nearly 60-day period abroad so far, he has signed several other decrees, including some authorising his government to sign loan agreements with international financial institutions.His absence sparked further speculation about his health, but the government has continually debunked reports that the head of state has been in hospital.Press freedom groups were outraged when it was announced two years ago that the media in Cameroon were banned from reporting on Biya's health.Cameroon's Communication Minister René Emmanuel Sadi has said the president is alive and will be returning to the country soon, during an interview with French-language broadcaster RFI.He also dismissed allegations by the opposition that the nonagenarian leader's absence amounted to a vacancy at the helm of the state, saying Biya continues to work from Geneva.But President Biya's continuing absence means Cameroon has a "glaring institutional vacuum", says the opposition CRM party's vice-president, Mamadou Mota."Executive power is exercised at the heart of the nation, not through smoke signals or telepathy from hotel suites on the other side of the world," he said last month.Additional reporting by Natasha Booty

schema.headline: Cameroon's President Biya reshuffles army amid unease at his long stay in Switzerland

title: Projectile sinks Indian-flagged ship off Yemen coast
description: Yemen's transportation ministry, part of the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government, accused ​the Iran-backed Houthis of carrying out the
body: Yemen's transportation ministry, part of the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government, accused ​the Iran-backed Houthis of carrying out the ​attack by using a boat laden with explosives, Reuters news agency reported.The group have not commented on the incident.The Houthis announced what it called a blockade on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports on 20 July.The UK Maritime Trade Operations ⁠agency has reported several attacks on ships in the region over the past week.Despite this, oil prices fell to a three-week low on Tuesday as senior US officials raised hopes of a deal with Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.In June, the US and Iran agreed on a 14-point Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to halt military operations and reopen the Strait, as well as to reach an agreement to end the war over the following 60 days.But three weeks after it was signed, US President Donald Trump declared the ceasefire "over" after Iranian attacks on ships in the strait, and US strikes in response.US officials said on Tuesday that talks have been progressing, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent suggesting a deal to reopen the Strait could be agreed as soon as Tuesday or Wednesday.Iran has said it is not negotiating with the US - and has no plans to do so - and is instead talking to Oman.

schema.headline: Projectile sinks Indian-flagged ship off Yemen coast

title: India CJP protests: Young women face online harassment and abuse
description: 'I was slut-shamed' - Indian women 'cockroach' protesters doxxed and abusedImage source, Hindustan Times via Getty ImagesImage caption, The women BBC
body: 'I was slut-shamed' - Indian women 'cockroach' protesters doxxed and abusedImage source, Hindustan Times via Getty ImagesImage caption, The women BBC spoke to say they received threats and abuses after participating in  the CJP protestsByZoya Mateen and Nikita YadavBBC News, DelhiTheir videos lasted only a few seconds: lip-syncs, sarcastic reels and jokes filmed on the way to protests.But while thousands of young people filled social media with memes and videos mocking Prime Minister Narendra Modi during one of India's biggest anti-government protest in years, many of the women behind those posts say they have paid a heavy price for speaking out.The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth-led movement that helped force the resignation of India's education minister, relied as much on Instagram as it did on marches. Memes, reels and viral videos became the movement's calling card, documenting everything from protest songs to the police crackdown when officers used tear gas and baton charges to stop demonstrators marching to parliament on 20 July. Delhi police said 60 protesters and 118 police personnel were injured on the day, but the CJP said the number of injured protesters was significantly higher than the official count.The posts reached hundreds of thousands of people, turning ordinary students into some of the movement's most recognisable faces.Since the protests ended, police have opened criminal cases against some protesters. But many women say another reckoning played out online. They describe rape threats, doctored images spreading on social media and strangers trawling through their photos and videos. Some cases spilled into TV debates, police complaints and political statements. Many more unfolded quietly, as young women deleted posts, locked their accounts and stopped answering calls from unknown numbers.The BBC spoke to four women and reviewed screenshots of abusive messages, posts and other material they shared. Their names have not been used to protect their identities.Content creatorI'm in my mid-20s. I had been posting about the protests from the beginning, but 20 July was the first time I attended one.After the baton charge that day and the internet shutdown around the protest site, I went home and started sharing first-person accounts on Instagram. I also helped organise food, aid and volunteers. I thought I was just helping and didn't think of it as political.But the hate started almost immediately.I was slut-shamed and I was attacked for questioning the prime minister's comments, external after the protest ended. [Modi said he forgave the children who had abused him, urging society to do the same rather than punish them or drag them through the courts.] I have lost count of the number of messages I have deleted and people I have blocked. But the comments keep coming.As a content creator, I already live with this feeling of constantly being watched. Every word I say is scrutinised, mostly by men.When I first started creating content, I would block men if they made me feel uncomfortable. Over time, the algorithm started pushing my content towards more women. I believe that has shielded me from abuse compared with many other female creators.And still, this happened.My mother stopped reading the comments on my posts long ago. She said she couldn't bear the things strangers were saying about her daughter. I understood. What parent wouldn't be frightened by that?As a woman in India, you grow up with fear. You're told not to stay out late, to watch where you go, who you're with and how you'll get home. You learn early that your safety is something you must constantly think about.When you have a voice online, that fear doesn't disappear. It just follows you there.Image source, EPAImage caption, Police used tear gas and baton charge to disperse protesters who tried to march to the parliament on 20 JulyCollege studentI am 20 years old, and this was my first protest. I went because I believed the students were standing up for something important. Before leaving the Metro station, I propped my phone against a railing and filmed a quick "fit check" [a video showing off her outfit before the protest.] "Going to get beaten by cops, guys," I joked. That's the kind of light-hearted videos I usually make.When police fired tear gas and charged protesters that afternoon, I kept filming. I was simply recording what was happening around me, as I always do. I never imagined those videos would reach far beyond my followers.I was wrong.One of them was shown on a national TV channel. Soon afterwards, my face began appearing in social media posts claiming protesters were being identified by the police. Someone even found out which college I attended. That's when I realised people weren't just attacking me online. They were trying to find me.My inbox filled with anonymous messages. Some said they would report me to the police so I would be beaten or arrested. Men called me degrading names associated with prostitution, made sexually explicit remarks, mocked my body and threatened violence. Some said I should be "taught a lesson". Others simply warned: "Your turn will come."What frightened me most wasn't the abuse itself, but what followed. Relatives and acquaintances called my parents, urging them to make me delete my videos or face the consequences. Seeing them so frightened was devastating. That's why I don't want my name published. I've since removed or archived almost all my protest videos.I worry less about what could happen to me than what they might do to my parents. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Several young women have faced online abuse and harassment after the protests Student activistI have always spoken my mind online. I'm a student activist and a Muslim, part of a religious minority in an increasingly polarised India. None of that ever frightened me.But after the CJP protests, everything changed.My Instagram account is private now. I've muted most of my other social media because the abuse has been unrelenting. Every time I look at my phone, there's another offensive comment or message or post about me.I went to the protest because I believed it was the right thing to do. I made a few satirical videos during the march. One mocked the prime minister. Others showed us singing on stage and chanting slogans. They were political, irreverent and the kind of videos I'd always made.But they spread far beyond the people I knew.One Instagram page edited a photograph to make it appear as though I was kissing a man to shame me. Another morphed my images and branded me an anti-national and a terrorist.I was also called a hijra - using the term for South Asia's transgender community as an insult - and dismissed as a paid protester.When my father, a journalist, read the comments, he panicked. He kept asking why I had spoken out. He said that once people saw my Muslim name, nothing else would matter. My parents have watched other Muslim activists investigated and arrested, and fear the same could happen to me.We live under constant dread. But I'm not going to stop speaking up. I still believe I was right to go to that protest. Now I just understand the cost much better than I did before.Image source, EPAImage caption, Memes and satirical short-form videos became a popular way for young protesters to speak about the movementStudentI'm a student in [the state of] West Bengal, where political discussions are an integral part of college life. I've participated in those conversations on campus for years, so I didn't think much before posting online about the protests.Although I first joined the Kolkata protest on 20 July, I'd already been helping online, organising supplies ranging from diabetic biscuits to masks for people worried about being identified. A friend and I also launched an Instagram fundraiser.But on 24 July, the police started detaining protesters in the state and we began talking about it online.That's when the hate really started. People began leaving spiteful comments on my fundraiser post; they called me a prostitute in private messages. They did not stop even after the protest had ended - and eventually I deleted the post.In the days that followed, the fear of being doxxed became real. I changed my name on social media, made my account private and blocked messages from people I didn't know.What hurt most was that none of my male friends faced the abuse I did. They expressed similar views but weren't targeted over their sexuality or subjected to insults about their mothers. I was.When it comes to women, the response quickly becomes about our gender. That's left me wondering why women can't express the same opinions as men online.

schema.headline: India CJP protests: Young women face online harassment and abuse

title: Nirmal Purja: How a generation of record-setting guides died in a disaster which klled a climbing legend
description: Purja, 43, also known as Nims, was the leading figure of the 10-member international team up Broad Peak, the world's 12th highest mountain, when the a
body: Purja, 43, also known as Nims, was the leading figure of the 10-member international team up Broad Peak, the world's 12th highest mountain, when the avalanche struck."Nims of course was iconic and undisputedly amongst the best of his generation," says Ben Ayers, a longtime Everest reporter for Outside Magazine.Kili Pemba Sherpa and Pur Bahadur Gurung, who were also guiding the Broad Peak expedition, were "strong climbers with a solid resume", Ayers said.Kili Pemba, 46, had just earned the coveted mountaineering Grand Slam after completing his last of the 14 highest peaks, also known as eight-thousanders, in early July.Even before this crowning achievement, he was already among the best in the industry having been part of the Nepali team, led again by Purja, that completed the first winter ascent of K2 in January 2021.At the time, K2, the world's second highest peak, was the only one of the eight-thousanders not yet climbed in winter. But at 8,611m, K2 is known to be steeper, more unpredictable and deadlier than Everest (8,849m).Many have described Kili Pemba as humble and deeply committed in serving his clients. He'd led two double-leg amputees, on separate occasions, to the summits of Everest and Manaslu, the eighth-highest mountain."That was the toughest task for any guide, [Kili Pemba] did that with a lot of care," says Gyanendra Shrestha, a government official who was at Everest Base Camp during one of these climbs.Pur Bahadur Gurung, 37, scaled 12 of the 14 highest peaks and was one of only 100 Nepali guides certified by the International Federation of Mountain Guides Association (IFMGA)."It takes a lot of money, passion and dedication to become an IFMGA guide. This tells us a lot about Pur Bahadur's zeal for mountaineering," says Himal Gautam, a spokesman for Nepal's tourism department. "It also speaks to the unprecedented loss we have suffered on Broad Peak," he adds.In 2024, Pur Bahadur was part of the team that discovered a century-old boot on Everest, believed to be that of British climber Andrew Irvine, who vanished on the mountain in 1924.The other three Nepali guides who perished on Broad Peak last week include Gyaljen Sherpa, best known for scaling the third-highest mountain Kanchenjunga three times in one season – a feat that some colleagues say deserves a Guinness World Record.Then there's Nima Sherpa, 36, who scaled four eight-thousanders in 2026 alone, and Nawang Thindu Sherpa, who in his 20s was among Nepal's rising generation of mountain guides.Some credit Purja for bringing Pakistan onto the radar of mountaineers through his feat of scaling the 14 peaks in just over six months, which was documented in a Netflix film."Nims' success gave many [guides] and foreigners the courage to believe that this mountaineering crown was truly possible," says Iswari Paudel, acting president of the Nepal Mountaineering Association."This has made Pakistan a major overseas base for Nepali Sherpas. And while helping foreign climbers fulfil their dreams, many guides have themselves completed the 14 peaks," Iswari says.Ayers, the Everest reporter, says Purja helped "publicise a new era of mountaineering" which in many ways helped "democratise mountain-climbing", but also "fuelled commercialisation and risk".Because of how remote Pakistan's mountains are, it is far more challenging to organise expeditions there – a feat that only the best guides undertake, Sherpas tell the BBC."We have to fix our own ropes, cut our steps into the ice, and set up camps as we go along," says Nima Rinji Sherpa. The 20-year-old set a new record in 2024 as the youngest mountaineer to summit the world's 14 highest peaks."Even in an era of commercial mountaineering, we experience real, old-fashioned mountaineering [in Pakistan]," he says.But because the region is hard to access, climbers usually attempt two to three mountains per trip, which makes the itinerary very tight, Nima Rinji adds.In Nepal, by contrast, mountaineering infrastructure is well-developed. The main trekking routes towards Everest are lined with family-run lodges that offer beds, hot meals and other facilities.Emergency evacuations are also generally easier in the Himalayas, where there is an integrated network of rescue helicopters and aid outposts at high altitude, whereas the Karakoram range, being more isolated, features fewer accessible landing zones."In the Pakistan mountains, getting the helicopters to base camp already takes a lot more effort, let alone flying them above high camps. "Therefore, the Sherpas who are capable of working in high-pressure situations, and who have diverse experiences and multiple skills are the ones who will operate in Pakistan," Nima Rinji says.While the Broad Peak disaster may spur calls to tighten safety standards, many believe it will do little to change high-altitude tourism."Generally, these tragedies cause a moment of concern... but then things go back to how they were. It's difficult to say with any conviction that any accident in the mountains is 'preventable' as the inherent danger is so high... and that's part of the appeal," Ayers says.The mountaineering community is drawn to high-risk pursuits, says Medhavi Gulati, a researcher specialising in high-altitude mountaineering."Often, it's the dangers and risk of death that attracts people," she says.The existing generation of mountain guides will continue to crave the global fame and world records that their predecessors have attained, she says. "I don't think that appeal will ever go away," she says."We've seen disasters like this one before, and nothing changed," says expert mountaineer and writer Alan Arnette, who pointed to how an ice avalanche on Everest killed 16 Sherpas in April 2014, and the 11 climbers who died on K2 in 2008 after a massive chunk of ice broke off."I doubt the Broad Peak incident will have a significant impact, given history. I hope I'm wrong," he says.

schema.headline: Nirmal Purja: How a generation of record-setting guides died in a disaster which klled a climbing legend

title: Kenya elephant deaths: Behind the poisoning and the pesticide mystery
description: Mysterious elephant deaths in Kenya raise questions around pesticides Image source, Getty ImagesByThomas MukhwanaAfrica correspondentReporting fromAmb
body: Mysterious elephant deaths in Kenya raise questions around pesticides Image source, Getty ImagesByThomas MukhwanaAfrica correspondentReporting fromAmboseliUpdated 00:13 BSTNews that the recent deaths of 15 elephants may have been caused by pesticides sprayed on tomato crops surrounding Amboseli National Park has raised concerns and questions in Kenya.Last week, the Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) said that some of the elephants that had died between 24 June and 24 July had shown signs of "partial paralysis" that pointed to poisoning from cyanide used in pesticides.But conservationists have told the BBC that, perhaps, is not the full story. Farmers we have spoken to in the area were also sceptical."We have stayed with this wildlife for decades and have never experienced this," Daniel Nina, who represents some of the landowners in the area, told the BBC."So that's why we are wondering why it is happening today."The tomato farms are found in the Kimana area, which is part of a corridor between Amboseli National Park and the Tsavo National Park in the south of Kenya.It is a vast area known as the Amboseli ecosystem, which straddles the border near Tanzania where more than 2,000 elephants move along in search of food and water.These farms thrive thanks to the streams from nearby Mount Kilimanjaro and supply markets in Kenya's capital, Nairobi, and beyond.Image caption, The 15 elephants were found dead outside the Amboseli National Park between June and JulyThe chief vet of Kenya's Wildlife Service, Dr Isaac Lekolool, told us that they had found traces of cyanide in samples taken from the elephants' stomachs.He says that they are not ruling out deliberate poisoning but it's impossible at this stage to tell what could have killed the elephants."It's difficult to tell because we've not seen these kind of cases before. It is almost like a one-off, and it was within a period of about a month," Lekolool said.Their working theory is that the elephants were exposed to the toxin through pesticides sprayed on nearby tomato farms."It could be unintentional. Maybe people are trying to do some controls of pests on their crops, and that could have been maybe a source."A 2024 report by Kenyan food safety initiative Route to Food found a farmer in Kimana area using an insecticide that had an "active ingredient" that was "a chemical compound of cyanide". Wangunyu Njuguna, the author of the report, said that despite being illegal in Kenya, some toxic agrochemicals were smuggled through the border with Tanzania."The biggest problem is we're not enforcing similar standards in the region," Njuguna said. "There is no-one checking what I go and buy across the border, so I can just go buy anything and walk through the border and no-one stops me."Highly hazardous substances are common on Kenyan farms and some have been linked to serious diseases. While regulations against illegal agrochemicals exist, there is weak enforcement and little attention paid to how they can affect animals.'It's not adding up'However, we have spoken to several wildlife conservationists who have questioned the initial findings of Kenya's Wildlife Service. Paula Kahumbu is a world-renowned conservationist who has worked with elephants for nearly 30 years. "We haven't got enough detailed information to have confidence in this claim that it's due to pesticides in crops," Kahumbu said."Some information has been released to the public but it's not adding up. Those elephants have to eat a huge amount to kill them."Other experts who did not want to be named said the pesticide theory was inconsistent with elephant behaviour. They said that males are more likely to raid farms as they usually take more risks than females and calves. However, only one of the 15 elephants affected was an adult male.Nina, the landowners' representative, added that unlike the latest incident, previous cases of poisoning in farms had affected zebras and antelopes, which raid the same areas. "How does cyanide kill the elephants and leave behind the zebras, antelopes and wildebeests, which are eating the grass together?" Nina asked.Image source, Peter Njoroge/BBCImage caption, Officials suggest that pesticides sprayed on tomatoes in nearby farms could have poisoned the elephantsHuman-wildlife conflict has persisted for decades in communities near conservation areas across Kenya.Stephen Michael, a tomato farmer in Kimana, says elephants and giraffes occasionally raid farms in the area."Elephants come from time to time from Tsavo and Amboseli. They destroy many farms, not just mine," Michael said."The last time elephants came, they destroyed cabbages and tomatoes. I lost cabbages worth almost $1,535 [£1,140]. That doesn't include tomatoes. I might start crying if I count that."Frank Pope, CEO of conservation organisation Save the Elephants, told the BBC the pressure on Amboseli's elephants was not ivory anymore."It's land use," he said.Farms and lodges are increasingly taking up land around the park which was previously used by elephants. It is such activities that Pope says worsen the conflict with wildlife."People are moving into areas where there's enough water to grow crops, and fertile soils, and those are the very areas that the elephants tend to use as well."Nobody knows for sure what's causing the elephant deaths now.The fear is that the remaining elephants and the people who live near them could still be at risk.

schema.headline: Kenya elephant deaths: Behind the poisoning and the pesticide mystery

title: Ceuta: EU calls for stronger borders after migrant crossings into Spanish territory
description: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has called for "united action" on border security after the chaotic influx of tens of thousands of
body: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has called for "united action" on border security after the chaotic influx of tens of thousands of migrants from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta last week.Spain ⁠estimates that about 69,500 migrants ​have now returned to Morocco, exceeding initial estimates of 50,000. The official death toll on the Spanish side of the border stands at 72, with 11 deaths on the Moroccan side.EU interior minister are holding emergency talks by video conference on Tuesday to discuss the issue.The scenes in Ceuta have strained relations among some of the EU's 27 member states.In a letter to Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, von der Leyen praised his "swift handling" of the crisis.But she added: "From this incident, it is clear that we must do more to further strengthen our borders at critical points."In response to the Ceuta crossings, Italy temporarily suspended the Schengen arrangement with Spain.The Schengen agreement eliminates border checks and now encompasses more than 450 million people and 29 countries in Europe.Finland and Denmark backed Italy's move, while Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš urged a temporary suspension of Spain's Schengen membership.In response, Sánchez said he had "serious concerns" about some European governments and pointed out that Ceuta was not part of the Schengen area.While most had shown "support and solidarity", he said other European governments had chosen to attack Spain, "driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance, or political interest".In her letter to the Spanish PM, von der Leyen warned that "the protection of all our external borders is a shared European responsibility", while calling for "vigilant monitoring and the use of physical barriers where needed".Tuesday's video conference will be a chance to draw "lessons" from the Ceuta episode, von der Leyen said, warning the challenges of illegal immigration require "a common European response, united action and solidarity".She urged the EU to "double down" in five areas: preventing irregular migration in the first place via cooperation with partner states; strengthening external borders; implementing early warning systems; dismantling smuggling networks and reinforcing returns.Sánchez has accused migrant traffickers of exploiting a decision recently made by the country's supreme court which constrained the government's right to immediately deport people who had arrived by sea.The country's Interior Minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, said on Saturday that the situation had almost returned to normal and the country was working on an inflatable barrier to prevent illegal migration via the water.Are you in Ceuta? Tell us what life is like there.

schema.headline: Ceuta: EU calls for stronger borders after migrant crossings into Spanish territory

title: Afghan boxer arrives at Greek court in connection with death of Scottish woman
description: Figure caption, Sharif Ahmadzai leaving court after the hearingByBen PhilipReporting fromAthens and Megan BonarBBC ScotlandUpdated 1 hour agoThe man s
body: Figure caption, Sharif Ahmadzai leaving court after the hearingByBen PhilipReporting fromAthens and Megan BonarBBC ScotlandUpdated 1 hour agoThe man suspected of killing a Scottish aid worker in Greece has appeared in court in Athens.The body of Elisabeth Jane Ross was found in a suitcase at an abandoned building on 18 July, days after she had been reported missing.Sharif Ahmadzai, who is 26 and from Afghanistan, was told during the private court hearing that he faces charges of homicide with intent, robbery and weapons offences.He made no comment and the case was deferred until Thursday, when it is expected that Ahmadzai will be formally charged.Homicide with intent is equivalent to a murder charge in Scots law.Ahmadzai was driven to court in a grey Hyundai i30 with blacked out windows for the hearing.Image source, FacebookImage caption, Elisabeth Jane Ross is believed to have been working with immigrants in GreeceHe was escorted from the court more than an hour later by police officers with their faces covered. He kept his head down as he walked from the building back to the car.Police said Ross - who is from Edinburgh and is known to family and friends as Lisa - had been volunteering with a refugee support group based in Athens.She arrived in Greece on 26 June and stayed in the Kertasini area of Piraeus until 10 July.Her body was found in the Kypseli district of Athens on 18 July.Police said the coroner's initial report failed to determine a cause of death, but more detailed examinations concluded it was an "obvious criminal act, likely asphyxiation".Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Sharif Ahmadzai, 26, arrived at the court building in a grey carThe BBC understands Ahmadzai, who left Afghanistan after being orphaned aged 15, lives in Greece with his American wife and their child.After leaving his home country, he travelled to Greece via Iran and Turkey, according to a video telling his story, external which was published by the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC).He then settled in a refugee camp on the island of Lesbos, where he met his wife and converted to Christianity.The couple then set up the charity Love Every Nation Athens to help other refugees.He won a Greek super lightweight boxing title earlier this year.The president of the Union of Police Officers of Southeast Attica, George Kalliakmanis, said it was "possible" Ross and Ahmadzai had crossed paths through charity work.He said they were investigating whether Ahmadzai had a key to the apartment Ross was staying in.The union said it had verified footage appearing to show Ahmadzai carrying a suitcase which is believed to have contained the body.It added that a location sharing app, used by Ahmadzai's wife, showed that the suspect had been at the property in Rethymnou Street where Ross is thought to have died.Kalliakmanis said Ahmadzai had admitted moving the body but denied murder, claiming he had found Ross dead in the bathroom.The officer said police believed the suspect took the victim's bank card and phone, and "made sure" to send text messages to her family and friends to "make it seem like she was still alive".He said the police also believed the suspect used the victim's bank card to make withdrawals totalling "around €10,000".Kalliakmanis added that Ahmadzai's wife had no involvement or prior knowledge of the alleged crime.Additional reporting by Daphne Toli in Athens

schema.headline: Afghan boxer arrives at Greek court in connection with death of Scottish woman

title: Ariana Grande has had enough of body comments, but 'scrutiny' will linger
description: Image source, Katia TemkinImage caption, Grande has cancelled appearances including a starring role in a stage musical in London next yearByIan Youngs
body: Image source, Katia TemkinImage caption, Grande has cancelled appearances including a starring role in a stage musical in London next yearByIan YoungsCulture reporterThree years ago, Ariana Grande made a plea for people not to comment about her body. Responding in a TikTok video to comments about her weight and figure, the pop star and actress told fans there were "many different ways to look healthy and beautiful".Three years on, and the social media speculation about her body and her health has continued. After "endless, ongoing public scrutiny", the star's spokesperson released a statement saying she "will be taking a step back from visibility" at the end of her current tour."She looks forward to finishing the tour and ending it on a high note, both healthily and happily," the statement stressed, "and then taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny."Image source, Babydoll Music/Republic Records/YouTubeImage caption, Grande released the video for her new single Petal on FridayIt follows the release of her eighth studio album Petal and the graphic video for its title track on Friday.The song refers to the pressures of fame, and the video shows Grande as a starlet who tries out for a group of talent scouts, dressing as a variety of different pop star personas. None are deemed good enough.The men initially inform her that it "couldn't hurt" to lose some weight, among other things, before they tell the final persona that they miss "the way you used to be".She then murders them all with a chainsaw."I wrote [this album] from a place that I don't usually, which was like an unfiltered rage," she has said.Whatever the message, the appearance is the thing that has attracted the most attention, and with many on social media saying the scrutiny comes from genuine concern. The comments and screengrabs flooded social media over the weekend.'Specimen in a petri dish'The top comment under the Petal video on YouTube said: "It's not about wanting the old Ariana back. It's about wanting her to be healthy."One fan wrote on X that she "has become so thin that people are genuinely concerned".Her loyal fans sent their support, making #Weloveyouariana trend on social media. Some criticised those who were focusing on her body. "No-one has the right to comment on anyone else's body or appearance," a user wrote.Music journalist Sophie Williams told BBC Radio 5 Live that the "constant commentary around her has really, really elevated over the weekend as she's been promoting new music"."So we're led to think in part that that [commentary] has brought us to this decision," she said.Grande is scheduled to continue the Eternal Sunshine Tour in Chicago this week before 10 dates at London's O2 arena, where the tour will finish on 1 September.Her "step back" means she will no longer star in Stephen Sondheim's stage musical Sunday in the Park with George opposite her Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey at London's Barbican in 2027.Grande has lived for more than 15 years - half her life - in the spotlight."I've been doing this in front of the public and been a specimen in a petri dish since I was 16 or 17, so I have heard it all," Grande told an interviewer, external during the press tour for the first Wicked film in 2024."I've heard every version of it, of what's wrong with me. And then you fix it, and then it's wrong for different reasons. But that's everything from – even just the simplest thing – your appearance, you know?"It's hard to protect yourself from that noise."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Grande was nominated for an Oscar in 2025 for playing Glinda in WickedGrande began singing at the age of eight and made her name as a teenage actress in Nickelodeon sitcom Victorious and its spin-off, Sam & Cat.Since releasing her debut single in 2011, she has scored 10 US number one hits and earned 20 Grammy Award nominations, winning three times.She has also made a successful move into acting, earning an Oscar nomination in 2025 for Wicked.But she has also experienced some difficult times.In 2017, 22 people were killed in a suicide bomb attack outside her concert at Manchester Arena.The following year, she said she was dealing with symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and that she wanted to "not be afraid" but added: "The truth is, it's scary. It's scary going anywhere. You look at places differently."When her ex-boyfriend, rapper Mac Miller, died in 2018, she later spoke about her "all-consuming" grief.Her relationships and break-ups have never been far from the headlines, including with comedian Pete Davidson, estate agent Dalton Gomez, her married Wicked co-star Ethan Slater, and former backing dancer Ricky Alvarez.In another new song, Oh Well, she says an unnamed ex or exes can "all go to hell".Elsewhere, she has also spoken about having depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and has called for mandatory therapy for child stars.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Grande has had 10 number one singles in the US and eight in the UKThis summer, she launched the Brighter Days Ahead Foundation, a mental health initiative to support groups including the crew and performers on her current tour."A lot of people perhaps forget that she's been famous for nearly 15 years, and she has a unique story in that she sadly lived out a lot of trauma in the public eye," Williams says."As fans and those working in music, all that we can do is wish her well," she told BBC NewsIn Grande's video appeal in 2023, she said that even if concerned onlookers thought they were "saying something good or well-intentioned" about someone's appearance and wellbeing, they should think twice."I think we should be gentler and less comfortable commenting on people's bodies, no matter what."The star also told fans that the period when they considered her to have looked the healthiest was in fact a time when she was on antidepressants while also drinking and eating poorly, so it was, in fact, "the unhealthiest version of my body"."Healthy can look different," she said. "You never know what someone is going through, so even if you are coming from a loving place and a caring place, that person probably is working on it or has a support system that they are working on it with."Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: Ariana Grande has had enough of body comments, but 'scrutiny' will linger

title: Washington wildfire arson suspect twice linked to other blazes, authorities say
description: Washington Governor Bob Ferguson said it was a "nightmare situation", adding: "This is likely the worst natural disaster in Spokane history." No death
body: Washington Governor Bob Ferguson said it was a "nightmare situation", adding: "This is likely the worst natural disaster in Spokane history." No deaths or injuries have been confirmed.But the city's mayor Lisa Brown said there was still "the potential for lives to be lost". Authorities are trying to make contact with 14 people they have been unable to reach by mobile phone, but are not yet considered missing.Sheriff John Nowels said it was likely many of them did leave but had lost signal or had depleted phone batteries.The three fires in the city - Old Trails, Fairview and Autumn Lane - are among a total of 16 wildfires in Washington state, according to the state's department of natural resources.Firefighters have made progress against two of them, but while Tuesday saw lighter winds and cooler weather, temperatures could rise again later this week. Farinacci, who was arrested over the Old Trails fire, was being held on a charge of arson in the first degree. He was held on a $1m (£744,000) bond. He appeared in court on Tuesday via video call, but did not enter a plea to the charge. Residents reported seeing Farinacci near some train tracks before they saw flames in the area, according to charging documents. Authorities stopped Farinacci near the scene. He was found with a pack of cigarettes, a butane lighter and a box of what authorities called "heavy duty waterproof matches", say the court papers. He spoke with authorities and denied starting the fire or being in the area where it started, saying witnesses who saw him didn't know "the whole thing". He was initially let go by authorities as they investigated the cause of the blaze. Fire officials eliminated other possible causes, like train activity or electrical infrastructure, and found it likely to be caused by vegetation with ignition by matches or a lighter.Court records reveal Farinacci came under scrutiny from authorities in two other arson investigations for fires last summer, though he was never charged. Sheriff Nowels said the Spokane resident also has a manslaughter conviction. Farinacci, then aged 21, shot and killed his father in 2010, according to court records cited by US media outlets. He pleaded guilty to manslaughter and was released from prison in 2020.  Buildings, including homes and businesses, have been destroyed, with videos from the city showing flames tearing through houses as helicopters fly above, trying to put out the flames. Resident Anna Andreachi, who has lost her home, told BBC News partner CBS News: "All of our memories are gone. "My dad just died, and all of his stuff was still in there, too."  One man who saved his home by digging a fire line said he felt "survivor's guilt" after his neighbour lost theirs. "We're going to open our home to our neighbours," Joe Cvancara said. "I know it's going to take a long time to rebuild."More than 900 firefighters have been assigned to the Washington fires, with reinforcements expected from other states soon. Wildfires have also been burning north of Washington state in Canada's British Columbia, where more than 8,000 people have been evacuated and over 230 homes have been destroyed.It comes as the province's interior region deals with extreme drought conditions, and as temperatures in the Okanagan are expected to hit a high mid-30C (86F). More than 100 fires were started last week alone amid the hot and dry weather, officials in British Columbia said.Scientists have said that human-induced climate change makes the warm, dry conditions that lead to wildfires more likely - as well as leading to more frequent and intense heatwaves and potential summer droughts.With additional reporting from Nadine Yousif in Toronto.

schema.headline: Washington wildfire arson suspect twice linked to other blazes, authorities say

title: How to avoid the worst of the Italian heatwave this summer
description: Image source, ReutersByMalu CursinoTemperatures across Italy are soaring to levels deemed threatening to people's health and wellbeing. Looking ahead
body: Image source, ReutersByMalu CursinoTemperatures across Italy are soaring to levels deemed threatening to people's health and wellbeing. Looking ahead to Thursday, the ministry of health has issued a red alert for all of Italy's 27 major cities, external, including popular tourist destinations Milan, Naples, Venice and Rome.As Europe's holiday season continues, the BBC spoke to experts about how to make the most of Italy during this latest heatwave.While some Italians say the current heat is "not a new phenomenon" given climate change, others from southern Italy have voiced their shock when visiting northern cities and towns.Time your outingsVisiting outdoor attractions during Italy's hottest hours (after lunchtime) is a "big mistake", Simone Quilici, director of the Archaeological Park of the Colosseum, tells the BBC.The Colosseum is not prescriptive about when people should visit, instead directing visitors to guidance from the regional authorities.To make visits cooler, the ministries of tourism and culture are allowing some attractions to stay open into the evening.Last week the government shared these additional opening hours, external during August:Colosseum (Rome) - open Fridays and Saturdays between 19:45 to 23:30Pantheon (Rome) - open from 19:00 to 23:00 every day except ThursdaysSforza Castle (Milan) - open from 17:30 until 19:30Image source, ReutersIn the Colosseum, cooling fans with mists have been set up in the entrances. Staff have also increased the number of medical stations available for emergencies. While temperatures are high, Rome has become used to it, Quilici says, explaining this is not an isolated situation but the "global phenomenon" of climate change.In his role as director of the Archaeological Park of the Colosseum, Quilici says he is in talks with archaeologists to introduce more shade-providing vegetation.Also in Rome, Mateo Medina says his team have introduced tours from 22:00 until midnight. Medina, director of operations at Vivicos International Travel, has also seen higher demand for 08:00 tours.Seek out parks, museums and churchesAir conditioned museums are unsurprisingly top of the heat-escaping list. Visiting some of Italy's many churches is another way to shelter from the heat, while absorbing the Catholic nation's heritage.Cooking classes and wine tasting sessions - usually hosted in venues with air conditioning - are becoming a popular alternative to walking tours, Medina says.He also recommends the capital's parks - villa Borghese, villa Adriana, Parque de Acquedotti - for shade, and visiting the underground Catacombs of San Sebastian and San Callisto.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Locals and tour guides who spoke to the BBC recommend sheltering from the sun during Italy's hottest hoursMarco Carrino, a tour guide in Naples, warns against visiting open archaeological sites during the hottest hours of the day. Many of his tours are to Pompeii. He recommends getting up early or, if possible, avoiding the hotter months altogether. He also encourages tourists to head to the National Archaeological Museum of Naples, which he says is "very important for archaeology and has a great Roman, Egyptian and even Greek collection".For Italian travel expert and writer Alessia Armenise, supermarkets are an underrated gem. As well as being air conditioned, she says you can do what she does and head to their deli counters and grab a reasonably priced, fresh and made-to-order sandwich "instead of queuing for those silly focaccia places that honestly taste the exact same". Go off the beaten track, and book aheadImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Enjoying a Sicilian granita - or Rome's grattachecca - is another way to stay coolIf you are somewhere in Italy with a natural body of water, or any water feature, plan your activities around it, Armenise says."Instead of walking, get a boat," she says. "Sometimes you will see things you cannot access via land."Instead of hiking a coastline, you can see it from the sea, she explains, with the added bonus of cooling water splashing on you.For Dr Agata Chrzanowksa, an art historian and tour guide in Florence, the hills and mountains north of the city are "a very good spot to runaway from the heat" for those driving. She highlights the Garfagnana region in particular.If seeing attractions like the Vatican in Rome is a non-negotiable, Armenise suggests booking in advance to avoid waiting in line in scorching temperatures.Several landmarks sell tickets online ahead of time. However, you need to be organised as tickets tend to sell out quickly, Medina says.Do as locals doWhile world-renowned attractions like the Colosseum might be top of your list, it's worth trying out local galleries and museums in smaller towns and cities which will often be less crowded and have a cafe where you can stay for hours, Armenise says.In a recent trip to Bologna, the travel writer felt so warm one evening that she decided to head to the cinema.While watching a film is something you could do back home, she says people might stumble on an old theatre which is "still a part of the history of that city".If you find yourself in Verona in need of an evening activity, she suggests a concert at the Verona Arena, an amphitheatre in the city centre.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, One of Florence's tour guides suggests heading to the Odeon cafe and bookstore to cool downDr Chrzanowksa, asked if she can share any local tips, suggests Florence's Odeon cafe and bookstore.She describes it as a "recently modernised art-nouveau cinema/theatre transformed into a beautiful bookshop where you can order and drink, with air con, and relax a little bit with books around you".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, As someone used to the heat, Giusto says "the best advice I can give is simply good common sense when visiting Venice in the summer"Venetian tour guide Fiona Giusto, who runs Venice Tours, plans most of her routes around shaded stopping spots. Like other tour guides, Giusto always urges tourists to stay hydrated, wear a hat and sunscreen.To get some culture without the heat, she suggests heading to Venice's Teatro La Fenice - a historic opera house - and the Ca' Rezzonico art museum. "The best advice I can give is good common sense," she adds.

schema.headline: How to avoid the worst of the Italian heatwave this summer

title: Armed man arrested at Trump's golf course ahead of president's visit
description: Authorities in California have arrested a man who was seen near a golf course owned by President Donald Trump in the Los Angeles area, ahead of the pr
body: Authorities in California have arrested a man who was seen near a golf course owned by President Donald Trump in the Los Angeles area, ahead of the president's visit for a fundraising dinner there. Jeanine John Taele, 38, was found with a pistol and illegal ammunition at the Trump National Golf Course in Rancho Palos Verdes, investigators say.According to the Los Angeles Sheriff's Department, he was "observed walking throughout the golf course grounds taking photographs and videos and appearing to monitor security-planning activities".The arrest took place on Sunday afternoon. Trump is currently visiting California to attend a Republican party fundraising dinner at the course on Tuesday.Taele is being held on charges of carrying a concealed firearm and possession of armour-piercing/prohibited ammunition. In a news release, the sheriff's department said Taele was arrested after plainclothes federal agents reported a suspicious person to local authorities during the middle of the day, around 1530 ET (2330 BST). When police confronted the man, they discovered that he was being sought in connection to a robbery by the El Segundo Police Department, about 15 miles (25km) north of Rancho Palos Verdes, a wealthy coastal enclave known for its hills and scenic cliffs. Authorities searched him and found he was carrying a 16-round magazine containing hollow point ammunition. In his vehicle, which was parked at the golf course, they found a loaded pistol, along with a loaded magazine containing hollow-point ammunition. Hollow point bullets flatten and widen on impact, causing maximum damage to vital organs. California, which has some of the strictest gun laws in the US, has banned magazines capable of holding more than 10 bullets. The suspect's home in Downey, a city also in the LA-area, was raided on Monday by agents from the FBI's Joint Terrorism Task Force and the LA County Sheriff's Department Major Crimes Bureau.The sheriff's department said his home was searched due to the "potential security implications surrounding the incident". Inside his home, they found an "illegally modified AR platform rifle" a .45 pistol, body armour, high-capacity magazines, a plethora of bullets for pistols and rifles and multiple notebooks "containing concerning statements". The investigation is continuing, with assistance from the US Secret Service, and officials say more charges may be filed later.The sheriff's statement adds that they have not identified any "credible threat to our communities"."However, this case underscores the importance of vigilance, strong partnerships with local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies, and the proactive steps taken to identify and investigate suspicious activity before it can escalate."The arrest happened during a rare visit to California by the president. He is planning to attend a Republican fundraising dinner at his golf courseAccording to the White House, Trump was due to give a speech critical of California Governor Gavin Newsom, who is widely considered to be planning a run for the presidency in the 2028 election, after Trump's second term ends.On Wednesday, Trump is travelling to Las Vegas to deliver a speech at a casino.The visits come as campaign activity ramps up ahead of the mid-term elections in November, when the balance of power in Congress is up for grabs.Trump has survived three assassination attempts in recent years. After the most recent, when a gunman stormed a hotel in Washington during a White House dinner, Trump's security team said they would review their protocols for protecting the president. Officials have not said whether the suspect in Rancho Palos Verdes was seeking to hurt Trump and he is not facing any criminal charges related to such allegations.

schema.headline: Armed man arrested at Trump's golf course ahead of president's visit

title: Ethiopia landslide at Amhara's Tsadqane Debre Mitmaq St Mary Monastery kills 14
description: Funerals have been held for some of the 14 people killed in a landslide that hit a mountain monastery hosting an overnight prayer session in Ethiopia'
body: Funerals have been held for some of the 14 people killed in a landslide that hit a mountain monastery hosting an overnight prayer session in Ethiopia's northern Amhara region.Rescue efforts for others feared trapped in the debris after a hillside above the Orthodox Church monastery collapsed in the early hours of Monday morning have now been halted.The monastery includes a prayer chamber carved into the mountainside, where the worshippers had gathered for the special prayer service."The land above the cave… slid after the heavy rain that lasted throughout the night," Dagnachew Azbite, a senior local official, told the BBC.Seven people had been found injured, five of them seriously, he said.The prayer service being held at the Tsadqane Debre Mitmaq St Mary Monastery included a holy water cleansing ritual that is popular among Orthodox Christians seeking spiritual healing for chronic illnesses."Many of those who died had gathered to receive the holy water," Megabe Hadis Neka Tibeb Ababu, the diocese's general manager, told the Associated Press news agency.Eleven of those who died have been buried at the monastery, while the bodies of the others have been returned to their hometowns for burial, according to Megabe.Identifying some of the victims remained a challenge, he said.Emergency teams, security personnel, healthcare workers and nearby residents had been among those carrying out search and rescue operations at the site, the local authorities said.Archbishop Abune Klementos, the head of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church's North Shewa Diocese, travelled to the monastery to lead funeral prayers for those killed, pray for the injured and offer comfort to grieving families, the authorities added.Landslides are a recurring hazard in Ethiopia during the country's main rainy season, which typically runs from June to August.In March, more than 100 people were killed in floods and landslides triggered by heavy rains in the southern Gamo Zone area. More than 229 people, including rescuers, were killed by a landslide in the neighbouring Geze Gofa Zone in July 2024, which was one of the country's deadliest weather-related disasters in recent years.Over the past two decades, numerous studies have documented a rise in both extreme wet spells and prolonged dry periods across East Africa, external.Scientists have repeatedly cautioned that human-driven climate change is making severe weather events - such as intense, long-lasting downpours - more frequent and more severe.Additional reporting by Wycliffe Muia

schema.headline: Ethiopia landslide at Amhara's Tsadqane Debre Mitmaq St Mary Monastery kills 14
